The image visibly shows severe perioral and oral herpetic lesions, satisfying the include criteria. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Clinical photograph of a human patient's left labial lesion, captioned as a hypertrophic HSV-2 genital lesion that progressed over two months. The article title and in-text mention confirm HSV-2 in an HIV-infected woman. The hypertrophic, granulomatous morphology is a recognized less-common (variant) presentation of genital herpes rather than classic grouped vesicles. [raw subtype: HSV-2] b: Photomicrograph of a punch biopsy from the same patient's left labial lesion showing the classic HSV cytopathic effect (glassy nuclear chromatin and multinucleation) on H&E, directly supporting herpes simplex attribution. [raw subtype: HSV-2]

in_text_mentions: 1 × 3 cm granulomatous lesion developed on the left labia. This was associated with surrounding tissue edema, and shotty left inguinal lymphadenopathy, and progressed over the subsequent two months (Figure 1(a)). panels.rationale: Caption states 'Genital herpes in a female patient' and article title confirms genital herpes mimicking donovanosis; in-text describes large confluent vulvar ulcerative lesions visible in image. Donovanosis was only differential, not final diagnosis. Presentation is large chronic ulcers in HIV-positive patient, atypical for classic grouped vesicles.

in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed multiple large, confluent, erythematous, ulcerative lesions involving the vulvar region, with the largest measuring approximately 5-6 cm in diameter. The lesions were predominantly superficial, with areas of deeper ulceration (Figure 1). The ulcer base was bright erythematous, denuded, and moist, with focal areas of whitish exudate. The borders were irregular but relatively well-demarcated, without obvious rolled or indurated edges. Initially, the differential diagnoses included vulvar cancer, genital herpes and donovanosis.

panels.rationale: Single H&E histology panel from a biopsy of the lesion in an article whose title is disease-focused (pseudotumoral genital herpes simplex virus infection). The panel is a real human-patient image and the annotated ulcerated epidermis with dermal acute inflammatory and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate belongs to a genital herpes simplex lesion, so disease attribution to herpes_simplex is supported by the title plus the captioned manifestation. The pathognomonic multinucleated giant cells are explicitly assigned to Figure 3 and the HSV immunostains to Figure 4, so they are not tagged here; the panel is an unusual (pseudotumoral) presentation, hence atypical. No ethnicity or age is stated; Fitzpatrick tone is not assessable from an H&E section.

Along the base of the ulceration were epidermal cells demonstrating viral cytopathic changes and multinucleated giant cells (Figures 3(a) and 3(b)). These cells stained positively with HSV-1 and HSV-2 immunostains (Figures 4(a) and 4(b)). Cytomegalovirus (CMV) immunostain, Epstein-Barr virus (EBER) in situ hybridization, and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) and Fite stains were negative. Viral cultures of the lesions were negative.
